title: The Last Normal Tuesday
synopsis: Examines Australia's housing bubble, manufacturing collapse, and AI-driven job displacement, arguing that unprecedented economic disruption is imminent.

content:
I've been walking through Sydney lately with a growing sense of unreality. The city itself remains stubbornly and beautifully physical. What unsettles me are the numbers floating above it - invisible, and somehow more consequential than the buildings they're attached to.

A terrace in Surry Hills, thirty-eight square metres of ageing timber, sold recently for 1.3 million dollars. That's roughly thirty-four thousand dollars per square metre. I keep trying to hold that figure next to actual people earning actual wages and making actual decisions about their lives, and the connection keeps sliding away from me.

Since 1975, Sydney house prices have risen about 4,645 percent. Wages over the same period have risen 1,183 percent. The median house now costs nearly ten times median annual income, where in the 1980s the ratio was closer to four. I walked past a five-bedroom terrace in Paddington with a buyer's guide of ten million dollars; similar houses in that street sold for fifty thousand in the 1980s.

These aren't only statistics. They describe a change in what it means to live here. The assumption that work leads to security, that each generation does a little better than the last, that there's a place for you if you're willing to earn it - none of these were ever guarantees, but they were reasonable things to expect, and they're becoming fantasies within a single lifetime.

**Two Curves Meeting**

Housing is only half of it, and I suspect the smaller half.

The consultancy reports estimate 1.3 million Australian workers will need to move into new careers by 2030, with a third of the workforce facing potential displacement. Those projections assume AI capability plateaus, that progress stays roughly linear, and that there'll be time to adapt. I don't believe any of the three.

What I actually observe is capability doubling every few months. Customer service departments that existed last year have gone. Law firms are cutting junior positions by forty percent. Accounting graduates can't find work because the tasks they were hired for are done for a fraction of the cost. These are current events, not forecasts.

And the jobs that were supposed to be safe - the knowledge work, the analysis, the skilled professional roles - are precisely the ones this technology reaches first. The cognitive ladder that previous generations climbed, where a displaced factory worker retrained into administrative work, is losing rungs faster than anyone can climb them.

I think these two curves are usually discussed as separate problems, and they're the same problem. A country that stores its wealth in the price of its houses rather than in its capacity to produce things has nothing underneath the prices except the shared assumption that they'll keep rising. Change the nature of work and you find out what was actually holding it up.

**Norway, and What We Did Instead**

I think often about Norway. They found oil in 1969 and, rather than treat it as a windfall to spend, they built the Government Pension Fund Global. It holds 1.7 trillion dollars today - roughly 300,000 dollars for every Norwegian - and it generates returns sufficient to finance an entire national transition to a post-carbon economy while sustaining some of the highest living standards on earth.

Australia has uranium, coal, gas, iron ore, lithium, rare earths, gold, and agricultural land capable of feeding much of Asia. Our sovereign wealth fund holds 230 billion dollars, or 8,800 dollars per Australian. Their insight had nothing to do with geology. They worked out that a windfall spent on consumption disappears while a windfall invested compounds, and we've had fifty years to notice the same thing and have used them otherwise.

The manufacturing picture is worse than most people realise. From twenty-eight percent of GDP in the 1960s to under six percent today, the lowest in the OECD. We rank 102nd globally in economic complexity, between Bangladesh and Senegal. We import eighty-five percent of our medical devices and ninety percent of our pharmaceuticals. We cannot manufacture an EpiPen. When Ford, Holden and Toyota left in 2017 they took 120 supplier companies with them, and since 2022 energy costs have closed 1,400 more manufacturers - including Oceania Glass after 169 years, and Qenos, the only plastics manufacturer we had.

The standard defence is comparative advantage: a country should do what it's best at, and we're best at digging. I've never found this convincing, because it quietly assumes you can always buy what you don't make, which assumes the seller will always sell. The argument works perfectly in every decade except the ones where it matters.

**Four Words**

There's one change I'd make ahead of all the others, and its appeal is that it's almost embarrassingly small.

Lifting the nuclear prohibition requires deleting four words from the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act. Four words. Whatever anyone thinks about nuclear power on the merits - and there's a real argument to have about cost and timelines - a country sitting on roughly a third of the world's uranium, with the most geologically stable terrain on the planet, having banned itself from the technology by accident of a 1998 political compromise, ought to at least make that decision consciously rather than inherit it.

I raise it as the smallest possible demonstration of the larger point. Nothing about our position is structural. The tax settings were chosen, and they currently tax a young person's labour at the highest rate in the system while taxing the appreciation on a fourth investment property at half. The energy prices were chosen, and those 1,400 manufacturers didn't close because Australians stopped wanting glass and plastic. The manufacturing decline was permitted, year after year, by people who could have acted and decided it wasn't urgent. Every element of this was assembled out of decisions, which means it can be disassembled the same way, by people willing to make better ones.

I don't know precisely what Tuesday morning looks like five years from now, and I'm wary of anyone who says they do. Property prices detached from any economic foundation, AI displacing workers faster than they can adapt, and a manufacturing base that has effectively ceased to exist - that combination has no obvious precedent, and the honest position is that nobody has modelled it because nobody has seen it.

But I don't want to write about this as though it were weather. We still have the resource revenue to fund a correction, and we still have the decade in which to make one. Tuesday morning is coming either way. I'd much rather we spent the years before it building something than explaining to each other why it was always going to be fine.
